original_question: Give an elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes p such that neither p-2 nor p+2 is prime; in other words, prove by elementary means that infinitely many primes are not twin primes.
target_in_paper: Section 2009.2.5 (Kent Boklan), inside 2009.2 "Problem Session II": "How do you show there are infinitely many primes which are not twin primes." ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the mathematical core of the Boklan problem almost verbatim: it asks for an elementary proof of the infinitude of primes that are not twin primes, and it correctly glosses this as primes p for which neither p-2 nor p+2 is prime. ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, define what "not a twin prime" means: a prime p that does not belong to any twin-prime pair, i.e. both p-2 and p+2 fail to be prime. The paper itself uses the shorter phrase "primes which are not twin primes." ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

The requirement that the proof be "elementary" is essential and should be kept explicit. In the nearby context, Boklan says he wants to "do elementary things" and rejects the easy argument from Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, noting that primes of the form 15k + 7 would give a trivial proof but that "Dirichlet isn't elementary." ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

The paper asks only for an existence proof of infinitude; it does not ask for a density result, asymptotic count, quantitative lower bound, or any statement about proving the twin-prime conjecture itself. ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

The ambient setting is the ordinary integers and prime numbers; no extra notation, parameters, or auxiliary hypotheses are introduced in this problem entry. ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
refined_question: Give an elementary proof that infinitely many prime numbers are not members of any twin-prime pair; that is, prove that there exist infinitely many primes p such that both p-2 and p+2 fail to be prime. The proof should be elementary in the sense intended in the paper, avoiding non-elementary input such as Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.
justification: This paper is a collection of CANT problem-session notes, not a theorem/proposition paper with numbered statements such as Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the abstract and contents show that it records problems section-by-section, and the relevant item is the informal question posed by Kent Boklan in §2009.2.5. In that entry, the paper explicitly frames the goal as finding an elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes which are not twin primes, after mentioning Brun's theorem only as background and dismissing the Dirichlet-based proof as non-elementary. So the refined question should stay narrowly on that existence problem and keep the elementary-method requirement front and center. ([theoryofnumbers.com](https://www.theoryofnumbers.com/cant/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
